title: LLMs Can Design Near-Optimal OR Algorithms
hook: Given only a problem class description and a Python sandbox, a frontier model writes an algorithm that matches or beats the best known method — before ever seeing an evaluation instance.
key_points: Tests whether LLMs can design algorithms for well-specified operations research problems: inventory control, queueing network control, assortment optimization.
Level 1: the model gets one instance and returns a solution. Level 2: it gets only the problem class and parameter ranges, and returns an algorithm.
The strongest model tested, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best existing method on almost all evaluated instances.
This holds even at level 2, where the returned algorithm is fixed before any evaluation instance is seen.
Performance improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart.
Conclusion: frontier LLMs are now a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems.
content_html: Baek asks a sharp question with a sharp setup: can an LLM design a good algorithm for a well-specified operations research problem? The domains are classics with decades of specialized literature — inventory control, queueing network control, assortment optimization.
extra_html:
The two levels

At level 1 the model receives one problem instance and returns a solution for that instance. At level 2 it receives only a description of the problem class and broad parameter ranges, and must return an algorithm mapping instance parameters to solutions — fixed before any evaluation instance is seen. Human input is deliberately minimal: one untuned prompt describing the problem, plus a Python sandbox with a fixed compute budget.

The result

The strongest model tested, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best existing method on almost all evaluated instances — including at level 2. That is the claim that matters: level 1 could in principle be brute-force search over a single instance, but level 2 requires committing to a general procedure in advance.

Performance also improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart, which suggests the capability is moving fast rather than sitting at a ceiling.

Why it matters

The authors' framing is modest and useful: for well-specified operations problems, a single untuned LLM query is now a serious empirical baseline. That changes the bar for publishing a new method in these areas, and it is a concrete instance of a pattern worth watching — frontier models as a default comparison point in fields where the problem statement is crisp and a verifier is cheap.

flashcards.prompt: What is the difference between the paper's level 1 and level 2 evaluations?
flashcards.back_html: Level 1: the model sees one problem instance and returns a solution for it. Level 2: it sees only the problem class and parameter ranges and must return an algorithm, fixed before any evaluation instance appears.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the level-2 result the stronger claim?

choices.text: The algorithm is committed before seeing evaluation instances, so it cannot be tuned to them
Level 2 uses a larger compute budget than level 1
Level 2 allows human experts to refine the prompt

flashcards.explanation_html: Level 1 could be solving instances by search. Level 2 requires generalizing to a mapping from parameters to solutions — genuine algorithm design rather than instance solving.

flashcards.prompt: What does the paper suggest OR researchers should now do?
flashcards.back_html: Treat a single untuned frontier-LLM query as a serious empirical baseline for well-specified problems — a method that cannot beat it may not be worth publishing as an improvement.
